title: Game of Life
description: Brute force to optimized: computing into a separate next-generation board versus in-place old+new state encoding decoded in a final pass.

blocks.text: Given an m x n grid board representing Conway's Game of Life (each cell is 1 for alive or 0 for dead), compute the next state of every cell SIMULTANEOUSLY, applying these rules based on each cell's current 8 neighbors: a live cell with fewer than 2 or more than 3 live neighbors dies; a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbors survives; a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbors becomes alive. Update the board in place.

blocks.caption: Encode both the old and new state in each cell at once, then decode in a final pass

blocks.text: Given a binary grid, compute the next generation of Conway's Game of Life, where every cell's next state depends on how many of its (up to 8) neighbors are currently alive, with all cells updating simultaneously based on the current generation.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Room Full of People Deciding to Sit or Stand, All at Once
blocks.text: Like a room full of people each deciding, based on how many of their immediate neighbors are currently STANDING, whether to stand or sit next, with everyone deciding based on the CURRENT arrangement, not on decisions others have already started making. To do this without a second room to track new positions, each person could hold up both a hand (their old status) and a foot position (their new status) simultaneously, only fully committing to standing or sitting once everyone has finished observing the original arrangement.

blocks.caption: Encoding old+new state together lets neighbor counts stay accurate throughout a single pass

blocks.text: Before allocating a full separate board to hold the next generation, notice that only 2 extra distinguishable states are needed per cell to safely encode both its old and new value at once.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If cells were overwritten with their new 0/1 value directly during a single pass, later cells would incorrectly count some neighbors using their ALREADY-UPDATED (next-generation) values instead of their true original ones.

Observation 2: There are only 4 possible (old state, new state) combinations for any cell: (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1); the two "unchanged" combinations already have clear representations (0 and 1), leaving only the two "changed" combinations needing new encodings.

Observation 3: Encode "was alive (1), now dead" as -1, and "was dead (0), now alive" as 2; both values are clearly distinguishable from the plain 0/1 states, and crucially, checking whether the ORIGINAL state was alive can still be done correctly (abs(value) == 1 catches both a plain 1 and an encoded -1).

Observation 4: After every cell has been visited once (using only original-state information via this trick), a final decoding pass converts any positive encoded value to 1, and everything else to 0, yielding the pure next-generation board.

Recognizing that only a handful of extra encoded values are needed to safely preserve "old state" information while simultaneously recording "new state" in the very same cell is the key space-saving insight.
This is an in-place encoding technique: pack both the old and new state into the same cell using extra distinguishable values, avoiding the need for a full separate board.
Compute the next generation into a completely separate board, using the original board only for neighbor lookups, then copy the result back.

items: For every cell, count its live neighbors using ONLY the original board's values.
Based on the cell's current state and its live-neighbor count, compute its next state and store it in a separate result board.
Copy the fully computed result board back into the original board.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Neighbor counting reads only from the original board, since nextBoard hasn't been touched yet at the time each cell is processed.
The two Game of Life rules (live cell survival, dead cell birth) are applied directly based on the counted live neighbors.
The final copy-back step is what nominally achieves "in place", though a full O(rows*cols) auxiliary board is used internally.

blocks.text: Every cell's next state is computed correctly using only original neighbor values, so the result is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), visiting every cell and each of its up to 8 neighbors once.
Space: O(rows * cols) for the separate next-generation board.

Limitation: allocating a full separate board to safely preserve original values, even though it's copied back at the end, uses O(rows*cols) extra space, when a clever encoding can preserve exactly the needed information directly within the original board's own cells.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force uses a full separate board. Instead, encode both a cell's original state and its new state directly into the cell itself, using values beyond the usual 0 and 1: -1 for "was alive, now dead", and 2 for "was dead, now alive" (cells that don't change stay as plain 0 or 1). When counting a neighbor's live status, check abs(value) == 1, which correctly identifies the neighbor's ORIGINAL state regardless of whether it has since been encoded with a "changed" marker. After a single pass computes and encodes every cell's next state this way, a final decoding pass converts every positive value to 1 and everything else to 0.

In a single pass, for each cell, count live neighbors using abs(board[ni][nj]) == 1 (correctly reading original states even if already encoded). Apply the Game of Life rules: if a live cell should die, set it to -1; if a dead cell should become alive, set it to 2; otherwise leave it unchanged. After the full pass, do a final pass converting every cell to 1 if its value is positive, or 0 otherwise.
Encode both old and new state directly into each cell using extra distinguishable values, then decode in a final pass.

blocks.title: Decoding
blocks.text: Converting every positive value to 1 (and everything else to 0) gives the final board [[1,1],[1,1]], matching the expected next generation.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), across the encoding pass and the decoding pass combined.
Space: O(1) extra, using only the existing board's own cells for all needed information.

The key trick is that abs(value) == 1 correctly identifies a cell whose ORIGINAL state was alive, whether or not it has since been re-encoded to reflect a change (since -1 is used specifically for "was alive"). This means neighbor-counting remains accurate throughout the entire encoding pass, regardless of the order cells are processed in or whether some neighbors have already been updated. The final decoding pass then simply reads off the "new state" component of each encoded value (positive means alive, non-positive means dead).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A live cell (1) has < 2 or > 3 live neighbors","Encode as -1 (was alive, now dead)"],["A dead cell (0) has exactly 3 live neighbors","Encode as 2 (was dead, now alive)"],["A cell's state doesn't change","Left as its plain original value (0 or 1), needing no special encoding at all"]]}

items: Neighbor counting uses abs(board[ni][nj]) == 1 specifically so that a neighbor already re-encoded as -1 (originally alive) still correctly counts as having been alive.
The two encoded values (-1 and 2) are chosen to be clearly distinguishable from both each other and from the plain 0/1 states.
The decoding pass (board[i][j] > 0 ? 1 : 0) correctly resolves 1 and 2 (both positive) to "alive", and 0 and -1 (non-positive) to "dead".

blocks.text: When a "simultaneous update" problem requires reading original values while writing new ones into the same storage, encoding both the old and new state into a small set of extra distinguishable values is a powerful technique for achieving true O(1) extra space.

items: Overwriting cells with their final 0/1 next-state value directly during the main pass, causing later cells to incorrectly count some neighbors using already-updated values.

Using abs(value) == 1 incorrectly, or forgetting it entirely and instead checking value == 1, which would fail to recognize a neighbor that has already been re-encoded to -1 as having originally been alive.
Forgetting the final decoding pass, leaving the board in its intermediate encoded state (containing -1s and 2s) instead of pure 0s and 1s.

items: Explicitly explain why abs(value) == 1 is needed (to correctly read a neighbor's ORIGINAL state even after it has been re-encoded), since this exact detail is the crux of why the in-place encoding trick is correct.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Update every cell of a grid SIMULTANEOUSLY based on neighbor rules, in place with O(1) space" points toward encoding both the old and new state into each cell using a small set of extra distinguishable values, decoded in a final pass.

items: How would you handle an infinite board (the classic, unbounded version of Conway's Game of Life)? Only the live cells and their immediate neighbors ever need consideration; a sparse set-based representation (tracking only live cell coordinates) replaces the fixed-size grid entirely.

What if the grid needed several generations computed in sequence? Repeat the encode-then-decode process once per generation, since each full pass produces exactly the next generation's pure 0/1 board.

How would you handle boundary cells (at the grid's edges) differently, e.g., if the grid were meant to wrap around (toroidal)? Adjust the neighbor-index bounds checks to wrap using modulo arithmetic instead of simply discarding out-of-bounds neighbors.

An in-place state-encoding technique, conceptually related to Set Matrix Zeroes's repurposing of existing storage (there, the first row/column; here, extra encoded values within each cell) to avoid auxiliary space.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(rows * cols) time, O(rows * cols) space.
Optimized (in-place old+new state encoding): O(rows * cols) time, O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: In-place encoding of both old and new state per cell, using extra distinguishable values, decoded in a final pass
Core Idea: Encode "was alive, now dead" as -1 and "was dead, now alive" as 2, checking abs(value)==1 for original-state neighbor counting, and decoding positive values to 1 at the end
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: Only 2 extra encoded values are needed to safely track both a cell's old and new state within its own storage, avoiding a full auxiliary board
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Encode -1 (was alive) / 2 (was dead, now alive); check abs(value)==1 for neighbors; decode positive to 1
